Main.sentence: Human Rights Watch ( HRW ) is a nonprofit watchdog group headquartered in New York City.

The organization was founded in 1978 as ___E:Helsinki Watch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Watch)___ , whose purpose was to monitor the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ 's compliance with the 1975 ___E:Helsinki Accords U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Accords)___ .
Its separate global divisions merged into Human Rights Watch in 1988. The group publishes annual reports on the state of human rights in about 100 countries.

Human Rights Watch was co-founded by ___E:Robert L. Bernstein U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Bernstein)___ ,  ___E:Jeri Laber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeri_Laber)___ , and ___E:Aryeh Neier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryeh_Neier)___  as a private American ___E:NGO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGO)___ in 1978, under the name ___E:Helsinki Watch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Watch)___ , to monitor the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ 's compliance with the ___E:Helsinki Accords U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Accords)___ .  [non-primary source needed] Helsinki Watch adopted a practice of publicly " ___E:naming and shaming U:(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/name_and_shame)___ " abusive governments through media coverage and direct exchanges with policymakers.

Helsinki Watch says that, by shining the international spotlight on human rights violations in the Soviet Union and its European partners, it contributed to the region's ___E:democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy)___ transformations in the late 1980s.  [non-primary source needed]
Americas Watch was founded in 1981 while bloody ___E:civil wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_war)___ engulfed Central America.

Relying on extensive on-the-ground fact-finding, Americas Watch not only addressed perceived abuses by government forces but also applied ___E:international humanitarian law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_humanitarian_law)___ to investigate and expose ___E:war crimes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_crime)___ by rebel groups.

In addition to raising concerns in the affected countries, Americas Watch also examined the role played by foreign governments, particularly the ___E:United States government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government)___ , in providing military and political support to abusive regimes.  [non-primary source needed]
Asia Watch (1985), Africa Watch (1988) and Middle East Watch (1989) were added to what was known as "The Watch Committees".
In 1988, these committees united under one umbrella to form Human Rights Watch.

In April 2021, Human Rights Watch released a report ___E:accusing Israel of apartheid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_and_apartheid)___ and calling on the ___E:International Criminal Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court_investigation_in_Palestine)___ to investigate "systematic discrimination" against Palestinians, becoming the first major international rights ___E:NGO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization)___ to do so.

In August 2020, the Chinese government ___E:sanctioned U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_sanctions)___ HRW executive director Kenneth Roth—along with the heads of four other U.S.-based democracy and human rights organizations and six U.S.
Republican lawmakers—for supporting the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement in the ___E:2019–20 Hong Kong protests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Hong_Kong_protests)___ .
The five organizations' leaders saw the sanctioning, whose details were unspecified, as a tit-for-tat measure in response to the earlier U.S. sanctioning of 11 Hong Kong officials.

The latter step had in turn been a reaction to the enactment of the ___E:Hong Kong National Security Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Hong_Kong_national_security_law)___ in June.  In October 2021, The New York Times reported that HRW left Hong Kong as a result of the Chinese sanctions, with the situation in Hong Kong henceforth to be monitored by HRW's China team. The decision to leave came amid a wider crackdown on civil society groups in Hong Kong.

Pursuant to the ___E:Universal Declaration of Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights)___ (UDHR), Human Rights Watch opposes violations of what the UDHR considers ___E:basic human rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_human_rights)___ .

This includes ___E:capital punishment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment)___ and ___E:discrimination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrimination)___ on the basis of ___E:sexual orientation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_social_movements)___ .

HRW advocates freedoms in connection with fundamental human rights, such as ___E:freedom of religion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion)___ and ___E:freedom of the press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press)___ .

It seeks to achieve change by publicly pressuring governments and their policymakers to curb human rights abuses, and by convincing more powerful governments to use their influence on governments that violate human rights.

Human Rights Watch publishes research reports on violations of ___E:international human rights norms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_human_rights_law)___ as set out by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and what it perceives to be other internationally accepted human-rights norms.
These reports are used as the basis for drawing international attention to abuses and pressuring governments and international organizations to reform.

Researchers conduct fact-finding missions to investigate suspect situations, also using diplomacy, staying in touch with victims, making files about public and individuals, providing required security for them in critical situations, and generating local and international media coverage.

Issues HRW raises in its reports include social and ___E:gender discrimination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrimination)___ , ___E:torture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture)___ , ___E:military use of children U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_use_of_children)___ , ___E:political corruption U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_corruption)___ , abuses in ___E:criminal justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_justice)___ systems, and the legalization of ___E:abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion)___ .  [non-primary source needed] HRW has documented and reported various violations of the laws of war and ___E:international humanitarian law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_humanitarian_law)___ , most recently in Yemen.  [non-primary source needed]
Human Rights Watch also supports writers worldwide who are persecuted for their work and in need of financial assistance.

The Hellman/Hammett grants are financed by the estate of the playwright ___E:Lillian Hellman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Hellman)___ in funds set up in her name and that of her longtime companion, the novelist ___E:Dashiell Hammett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashiell_Hammett)___ .

In addition to providing financial assistance, the Hellman/Hammett grants help raise international awareness of activists who have been silenced for speaking out in defence of human rights.  [non-primary source needed]

Each year, Human Rights Watch presents the ___E:Human Rights Defenders Award U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Defenders_Award)___ to activists who demonstrate leadership and courage in defending human rights.
The award winners work closely with HRW to investigate and expose human rights abuses.

Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the ___E:International Freedom of Expression Exchange U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Freedom_of_Expression_Exchange)___ , a global network of ___E:non-governmental organizations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organizations)___ that monitor ___E:censorship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship)___ worldwide.
It also co-founded the ___E:Cluster Munition Coalition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_Munition_Coalition)___ , which brought about an international convention banning the weapons.
HRW employs more than 275 staff—country experts, lawyers, journalists, and academics—and operates in more than 90 countries.

Headquartered in ___E:New York City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)___ , it has offices in ___E:Amsterdam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam)___ , ___E:Beirut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut)___ , ___E:Berlin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin)___ , ___E:Brussels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels)___ , ___E:Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago)___ , ___E:Geneva U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva)___ , ___E:Johannesburg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg)___ , ___E:London U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)___ , ___E:Los Angeles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles)___ , ___E:Nairobi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi)___ , ___E:Seoul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul)___ , ___E:Paris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris)___ , ___E:San Francisco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco)___ , ___E:Sydney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney)___ , ___E:Tokyo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo)___ , ___E:Toronto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto)___ , ___E:Washington, D.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C.)___ , and ___E:Zürich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCrich)___ .  [non-primary source needed] HRW maintains direct access to most of the countries it reports on. ___E:Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba)___ , ___E:North Korea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea)___ , ___E:Sudan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan)___ , ___E:Iran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran)___ , ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel)___ , ___E:Egypt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt)___ , the ___E:United Arab Emirates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates)___ , ___E:Uzbekistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzbekistan)___ and ___E:Venezuela U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela)___ are among the handful of countries that have blocked HRW staff members' access.

HRW's former executive director is ___E:Kenneth Roth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Roth)___ , who held the position from 1993 to 2022. Roth conducted investigations on abuses in ___E:Poland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland)___ after martial law was declared 1981. He later focused on ___E:Haiti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti)___ , which had just emerged from the ___E:Duvalier dictatorship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duvalier_dictatorship)___ but continued to be plagued with problems.

Roth's awareness of the importance of human rights began with stories his father had told about escaping ___E:Nazi Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany)___ in 1938. He graduated from ___E:Yale Law School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_School)___ and ___E:Brown University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University)___ .
___E:Tirana Hassan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirana_Hassan)___ was the group's executive director from 2023  to February 2025.

Human Rights Watch and ___E:Amnesty International U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International)___ are both international non-governmental organizations headquartered in the North Atlantic ___E:Anglosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere)___ that report on global human rights violations.
The major differences lie in the groups' structures and methods for promoting change.
Amnesty International is a mass-membership organization.

Mobilization of those members is the organization's central advocacy tool. Human Rights Watch's main products are its crisis-directed research and lengthy reports, whereas Amnesty International lobbies and writes detailed reports but also focuses on mass letter-writing campaigns, adopting individuals as " ___E:prisoners of conscience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoners_of_conscience)___ " and lobbying for their release.

HRW openly lobbies for specific actions for other governments to take against human rights offenders, including naming specific individuals for arrest, or ___E:sanctions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions)___ to be levied against certain countries, such as calling for punitive sanctions against the top leaders in ___E:Sudan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan)___ who oversaw a killing campaign in ___E:Darfur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darfur)___ .
The group also called for human rights activists who had been detained in Sudan to be released.
HRW's documentations of human rights abuses often include extensive analyses of conflicts' political and historical backgrounds, some of which have been published in academic journals.
AI's reports, on the other hand, tend to contain less analysis, instead focusing on specific abuses of rights.
In 2010, ___E:Jonathan Foreman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Foreman_(journalist))___ wrote that HRW had "all but eclipsed" Amnesty International.
According to Foreman, instead of being supported by a mass membership, as AI is, HRW depends on wealthy donors who like to see the organization's reports make headlines.
For this reason, according to Foreman, it may be that organizations like HRW "concentrate too much on places that the media already cares about," especially Israel.
In 2023, HRW had revenue of $94.2 million.

In 2010, financier ___E:George Soros U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Soros)___ of the ___E:Open Society Foundations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Society_Foundations)___ announced his intention to grant $100 million to HRW over ten years to help it expand its efforts internationally.
The donation, the largest in HRW's history, increased its operating staff of 300 by 120 people.

In 2020, HRW's board of directors discovered that HRW accepted a $470,000 donation from Saudi real estate magnate ___E:Mohamed Bin Issa Al Jaber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bin_Issa_Al_Jaber)___ , owner of a company HRW "had previously identified as complicit in labor rights abuse", under the condition that the donation not be used to support LGBT advocacy in the Middle East and North Africa.
After The Intercept reported the donation, it was returned, and HRW issued a statement that accepting it was "deeply regrettable".

Human Rights Watch publishes reports on many different topics  and compiles an annual World Report presenting an overview of the worldwide state of human rights.

It has been published by ___E:Seven Stories Press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Stories_Press)___ since 2006; the current edition, World Report 2020 , was released in January 2020, and covers events of 2019.   World Report 2020 , HRW's 30th annual review of human rights practices around the globe, includes reviews of human rights practices and trends in nearly 100 countries, and an introductory essay by Executive Director Kenneth Roth, "China's Global Threat to Human Rights".

HRW has reported extensively on subjects such as the ___E:Rwandan genocide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide)___ of 1994,  the ___E:Democratic Republic of the Congo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo)___ ,  and the excessive breadth of ___E:U.S. sex offender registries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_offender_registries_in_the_United_States)___ and their application to juveniles.

In the summer of 2004, the ___E:Rare Book and Manuscript Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_Book_and_Manuscript_Library_(Columbia_University))___ at ___E:Columbia University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University)___ in New York became the depository institution for the Human Rights Watch Archive, an active collection that documents decades of human rights investigations around the world.
The archive was transferred from the Norlin Library at the ___E:University of Colorado, Boulder U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado,_Boulder)___ .
It includes administrative files, public relations documents, and case and country files.

With some exceptions for security considerations, the Columbia University community and the public have access to field notes, taped and transcribed interviews with alleged victims of human rights violations, video and audiotapes, and other materials documenting HRW's activities since its founding in 1978 as Helsinki Watch.

Some parts of the HRW archive are not open to researchers or to the public, including the records of the meetings of the board of directors, the executive committee, and the various subcommittees, limiting historians' ability to understand the organization's internal decision-making.
HRW has been criticized for perceived bias by the national governments it has investigated for human rights abuses.
Some sources allege HRW is biased against Israel in its coverage of the ___E:Israel–Palestine conflict U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel%E2%80%93Palestine_conflict)___ .

In 2014, two ___E:Nobel Peace Laureates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Laureates)___ , ___E:Adolfo Pérez Esquivel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolfo_P%C3%A9rez_Esquivel)___ and ___E:Mairead Maguire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mairead_Maguire)___ , wrote a letter signed by 100 other human rights activists and scholars criticizing HRW for its revolving-door hiring practices with the U.S. government, its failure to denounce the U.S. practice of ___E:extrajudicial rendition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraordinary_rendition)___ , its endorsement of the U.S. ___E:2011 military intervention in Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_military_intervention_in_Libya)___ , and its silence during the ___E:2004 Haitian coup d'état U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Haitian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat)___ .
